title: Stunning Sacrifice
reviewNotes: Montages, captions and native complete diagrams reviewed. Begin at the complete sixteen-piece diagram after Kf4 36 seconds: White Kf4/Qc8/Rf8/Bd3/d4/e3/g3/h4 against Kh6/Qg6/Bg4/d7/e6/f6/g7/h5. Native13 establishes the full reversed board. The offered queen goes to e4, despite caption d4. Both legal White replies to Qe4+ are covered: Bxe4 and Kxe4. After the pawn-check sequence, g5+ is not immediate mate: White must answer hxg5+, then fxg5# is actual mate. Native27/28/29 show that complete bishop-capture finish, including the white pawn on g5 and then Black f6xg5. Native34/35 illustrate the corresponding king-capture branch. The prior legal-only review stopped before the final recapture; it is preserved and corrected rather than silently discarded. A complete finite Black strategy checks every White reply through actual mate, with all sixteen root pieces retained. Earlier queen/bishop-capture blunders and king-escape alternatives before this root remain outside the proof.
transcript: Sometimes the most majestic moves can come out of thin air. In this position, it seems like black is simply lost. It is down a full rook and there is no way to fight back. If the queen tries to capture this bishop, this is actually a blunder because this is going to be a checkmate unless you sacrifice your queen back. And now white is completely winning. And the only other check that we have available is E5. But after D takes E5 and F takes E5, the white king actually runs away. And even if we try to chase it, there's nothing to chase and the king is simply going to find shelter. So it seems like black is completely hopeless here and it should just resign. But for once, black is not the fool in this position and it finds the stunning and beautiful queen to D4 check. a full queen sacrifice, but with a very specific idea in mind to take away the E4 square and create a new pawn check once the bishop takes, we cannot go G5 right away because the king simply runs away. So, we need to go back to the idea of E5. And after the pawn takes, again, let's not be hasty and take this because the king runs. Instead, once the white pawn is blocking his own lord, we now play G5. And this is going to be a beautiful pawn checkmate. And some of you might think, well, Peter, what after the king takes? Well, now black can play D5, pushing the king back, and there is the same exact sequence. If you want to be able to find these incredible moves, I suggest you check out Chess Mind AI.
